blackfin-chromis.text: A small damselfish of Indo-Pacific reefs. Groups gather along exposed outer reef slopes and rocky inshore reefs, feeding on zooplankton, especially tiny crustaceans called copepods.
blackfin-chromis.fact: These little damselfish gather in groups along outer reef slopes and feed on drifting zooplankton.

rainbow-wrasse.text: A fast, bright wrasse of Indo-Pacific reefs. Adults gather above shallow reefs and reef flats, picking zooplankton out of the water. Young fish stay closer to the reef, and their colours differ from those of adult males.
rainbow-wrasse.fact: Rainbow wrasse gather over shallow reefs to catch tiny drifting crustaceans, and spawn above the reef at dusk.

blue-tang.text: A surgeonfish of Caribbean reefs. Adults are a deep blue; the young are bright yellow. Schools sweep over the reef grazing algae, and a sharp scalpel-like spine at the base of the tail defends each fish.
blue-tang.fact: Young blue tangs are bright yellow; adults turn deep blue. A sharp spine at the base of the tail helps defend them.

facts.Length: Usually about 30 cm; recorded to 37 cm
facts.Habitat: Reefs, grassy and rocky areas, 2 to 40 m

french-grunt.text: A daytime reef schooler that spreads out over seagrass at night to feed on small crustaceans and worms. The name comes from the grunting sound it makes by grinding its throat teeth together.
french-grunt.fact: French grunts get their name from the grunting sound they make by grinding their throat teeth together.

facts.Length: Up to about 30 cm; commonly about 17 cm
facts.Habitat: Reefs and seagrass, shallow water to 60 m

stoplight-parrotfish.text: A parrotfish of Caribbean reefs. It scrapes algae off dead coral with a fused beak of teeth and excretes the ground rock as fine white sand, one of the sources of reef beaches.
stoplight-parrotfish.fact: Parrotfish scrape algae off dead coral and excrete the ground rock as fine white sand, one source of reef beaches.
stoplight-parrotfish.sourceTitle: NOAA Fisheries — St. Thomas/St. John Fishery Management Plan, stoplight parrotfish

pacific-hake.text: A slender silver hake that schools over the continental shelf and slope of the northeast Pacific. It rises toward the surface at night to feed on krill and small fish, and spawns off California.
pacific-hake.fact: Pacific hake rise through the water at night to feed, then return to deeper water by day.

facts.Depth: Most common around 50 to 500 m; adults also occur below 900 m

silver-hake.text: A schooling hake of the northwest Atlantic shelf and canyon edges. By day it holds near the bottom; at night it rises into midwater to chase shrimp and small fish.
silver-hake.fact: Silver hake hold near the bottom by day, then rise into midwater at night to chase shrimp and small fish.

facts.Length: Up to about 76 cm; males commonly about 37 cm

nassau-grouper.text: A heavy-bodied reef grouper that sits near ledges and caves, alone or in small groups, and ambushes fish and crabs. It gathers in large numbers at full moon to spawn, which made it easy to overfish; it is now critically endangered.
nassau-grouper.fact: Nassau groupers gather in huge numbers at full moon to spawn, which made them easy to overfish and left them critically endangered.

wreckfish.text: A big, dark, slow-moving fish that lingers near wrecks, ledges and rocky outcrops on the continental slope, which is how it got its name. A deepwater fishery works the Blake Plateau for it.
wreckfish.fact: Young wreckfish shelter near floating debris, while adults lurk in deep rocky caves and under ledges.

facts.Length: Up to about 2 m, around 1 m in the game

rattail.text: Grenadiers, or rattails, are deep-sea fish with a big head and a long tail that tapers to a point. Large eyes, a keen sense of smell and sensitive chin barbels help them find prey and carrion above the dark seabed. The genus Coryphaenoides occurs on continental slopes and abyssal plains.
rattail.fact: Rattail fish get their name from a body that tapers into a long, thin tail. They also go by the name grenadier.

facts.Length: 30 cm to over 1 m, depending on species

blob-sculpin.text: A large, soft-bodied fish of the deep North Pacific. MBARI has observed blob sculpins resting beside nests of pink eggs on rocky outcrops. The fish guard their eggs, keeping watch over patches of seabed that serve as deep-sea nurseries.
blob-sculpin.fact: Blob sculpins guard nests of pink eggs on the deep seabed, a rare glimpse of parental care in deep-sea fish.
blob-sculpin.sourceTitle: MBARI — Nurseries in the deep sea

cutthroat-eel.text: A cutthroat eel is named for the slit-like gill openings low on its throat. It cruises slowly over slopes and volcano flanks, scavenging and picking up small prey.
cutthroat-eel.fact: The cutthroat eel is named for the slit-like gill openings low on its throat.
cutthroat-eel.sourceTitle: Academia Sinica Taiwan Fish Database — Synaphobranchus brevidorsalis

mariana-snailfish.text: The Mariana snailfish is one of the deepest-living fishes known. It has a scale-free, tadpole-like body and swims in small groups over the trench walls, feeding on amphipods and other small crustaceans.
mariana-snailfish.fact: The Mariana snailfish is one of the deepest-living fishes known, with a scale-free, tadpole-like body.

facts.Length: Up to 22.6 cm standard length (excluding tail fin)

reef-shark.text: The most common large shark on Caribbean reefs. It patrols reef edges and drop-offs, mostly at dusk and night, hunting fish, and often rests on the bottom by day.
reef-shark.fact: Caribbean reef sharks patrol reef edges mostly at dusk and night, and often rest on the bottom by day.

blue-shark.text: A slender, open-ocean shark with long pectoral fins and an indigo back. It follows currents across whole ocean basins and dives deep after squid and fish.
blue-shark.fact: Blue sharks follow ocean currents across whole basins and dive deep after squid and fish.

facts.Depth: Surface to about 350 m, sometimes deeper

sixgill-shark.text: A large, ancient-looking shark with six gill slits and large green eyes that reflect light. It lives in deep water by day and rises toward the shallows at night to feed.
sixgill-shark.fact: The sixgill shark has six gill slits and large green eyes, and it can move into shallow water at night to feed.

facts.Length: Up to about 5 m, 3.6 m in the game

sperm-whale.text: The largest toothed predator on Earth. It dives for over an hour to depths beyond 1,000 m, finding squid in the dark by echolocation clicks that are among the loudest sounds made by any animal.
sperm-whale.fact: Sperm whales dive for over an hour to depths beyond 1,000 m, finding squid with echolocation clicks among the loudest of any animal.

humpback-whale.text: A baleen whale famous for the long songs sung by males. Humpbacks migrate between productive feeding grounds, where they eat krill and small fish, and warmer breeding grounds where they mate and calve.
humpback-whale.fact: Male humpback whales sing long songs, and the whales migrate between feeding grounds and warmer breeding grounds.

facts.Habitat: Open water, often near islands and reefs

sea-lion.text: A playful, agile eared seal of the California coast. It hunts fish and squid on dives of a few minutes and often investigates divers and boats.
sea-lion.fact: California sea lions swim with their powerful front flippers and steer with their rear flippers.

facts.Length: Males about 2.4 m, females about 1.8 m
facts.Dive depth: Usually under 100 m, can exceed 250 m

whale-shark.text: The largest fish in the sea. It filters plankton, fish eggs and small fish from the water as it cruises with its huge mouth open, and each animal's spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.
whale-shark.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish in the sea, and each one's spot pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.

facts.Habitat: Warm open water, often near reefs

weddell-seal.text: The southernmost breeding mammal. A Weddell seal dives for up to an hour or more beneath Antarctic sea ice, hunting fish and squid, and keeps its breathing holes open by rasping the ice with its teeth.
weddell-seal.fact: A Weddell seal keeps its breathing holes open beneath Antarctic ice by rasping at the ice with its teeth.

facts.Dive depth: Usually to 300 m, up to about 600 m

nanomia.text: Not one animal but a colony: dozens of specialised, genetically identical members strung along a stem. The nectophores at the top beat to swim, others feed or reproduce. MBARI records it from near the surface down to about 700 m.
nanomia.fact: Nanomia looks like one animal but is a colony of dozens of specialised members strung along a stem.

atolla.text: A deep-sea crown jelly with a dark red bell. When attacked it throws out a spinning ring of bright blue light, a burglar alarm that may call a larger predator to the attacker.
atolla.fact: When attacked, the Atolla jelly throws out a spinning ring of blue light, a burglar alarm that may call a bigger predator.

facts.Depth: About 500 to 5,000 m for Atolla species (MBARI)

comb-jelly.text: A lobate comb jelly in the genus Bolinopsis. Eight rows of beating plates move it through the water and split light into a rainbow shimmer. Its broad feeding lobes help collect tiny plankton. Different Bolinopsis species live in tropical, temperate and polar seas; northeastern Pacific animals include B. microptera.
comb-jelly.fact: Comb jellies move with eight rows of beating plates that split light into a rainbow shimmer.

facts.Habitat: Open water, surface to over 1,000 m

comb-jelly.sourceTitle: Johnson et al. 2022 — Speciation of pelagic zooplankton: Bolinopsis species

beebe-shrimp.text: Rimicaris hybisae swarm the Beebe black smokers at roughly 4,960 m on the Mid-Cayman Rise. Microbes associated with their mouthparts and gill chamber contribute chemosynthetic food; their diet also includes carbon from photosynthesis. Their dorsal eye detects light without forming images and may sense faint vent light or bioluminescence.
beebe-shrimp.fact: Beebe vent shrimp swarm black smokers at about 4,960 m, fed partly by microbes in their gill chambers.
beebe-shrimp.sourceTitle: Streit et al. 2015 — Rimicaris hybisae carbon sources

hawaii-shrimp.text: Rimicaris loihi is a small vent shrimp described from Kamaʻehuakanaloa (formerly Lōʻihi) seamount, where it gathers around warm, mineral-rich vents near the summit. It was originally described under the name Opaepele loihi.
hawaii-shrimp.fact: This small shrimp swarms around warm, mineral-rich vents near the summit of Kama'ehuakanaloa.

facts.Habitat: Warm vents on a young volcano

hadal-amphipod.text: A scavenging amphipod of the deepest trenches. It swarms to food that falls from above, and its digestive enzymes can break down wood and plant material that has sunk into the trench.
hadal-amphipod.fact: Hirondellea gigas scavenges in the Mariana Trench, where baited traps have collected these crustaceans nearly 11 km down.
hadal-amphipod.sourceTitle: Kobayashi et al. 2012 — Hirondellea gigas at Challenger Deep

sun-star.text: A many-armed sea star of the California slope, with thirteen or more broad arms radiating from a wide central disc. It crawls over mud and rock on rows of tiny tube feet.
sun-star.fact: California sun stars raise their arms into passing currents to catch krill, shrimp and even fish.

brittle-star.text: A large abyssal brittle star. Brittle stars move by whipping their slender arms in a rowing motion, unlike sea stars that glide on tube feet, and they drop an arm to escape a predator.
brittle-star.fact: Brittle stars row along on their slender arms, and drop an arm to escape a predator.
brittle-star.sourceTitle: University of Texas Marine Science Institute — Brittle Stars

long-tailed-cucumber.text: An abyssal sea cucumber with a tall tail-like extension that stands up from the rear of its body. It crawls across the mud, swallowing sediment and digesting the organic matter in it.
long-tailed-cucumber.fact: This sea cucumber stands up a tall tail-like extension while it crawls across the mud, swallowing sediment for food.

amperima.text: A small pink sea cucumber of the abyssal north Atlantic. In the Porcupine Abyssal Plain study it became hundreds of times more common after 1996, a population boom that followed changes in the food supply from the surface.
amperima.fact: After 1996, Amperima sea cucumbers became hundreds of times more abundant at a study site on the Porcupine Abyssal Plain.
amperima.sourceTitle: Uthicke et al. 2009 — A boom–bust phylum? (Amperima size and population changes)

squat-lobster.text: Munidopsis is a deep-sea genus of squat lobsters with a pale, often ghost-white body and long, spiny legs. Species live on mud, wood, bones and near vents, picking at whatever organic material they find.
squat-lobster.fact: Some Munidopsis squat lobsters have entirely white bodies and legs, a striking sight on the dark seabed.

facts.Group: Munidopsis, a genus with many species
facts.Habitat: Deep seabed, including wood falls and vents

squat-lobster.sourceTitle: New records of Munidopsis from deep waters off Taiwan

tubeworm.text: A tubeworm of the Juan de Fuca vents. It has no mouth or gut as an adult: bacteria in its body turn sulfide from the vent fluid into food, and the red plume at the top is full of the blood pigment that carries sulfide and oxygen.
tubeworm.fact: An adult tubeworm has no mouth or gut: bacteria inside its body turn vent sulfide into food.
tubeworm.sourceTitle: NOAA PMEL — Axial tubeworms and their bacterial food source

cold-water-coral.text: A reef-building coral that needs no sunlight. Its naturally white branches form dense thickets on the Blake Plateau. Over thousands of years, coral skeletons and trapped sediment build mounds that provide habitat for fish and other invertebrates.
cold-water-coral.fact: Cold-water coral needs no sunlight, and over thousands of years its skeletons build mounds that shelter fish, crabs and sponges.

brain-coral.text: A reef-building coral of the Caribbean. Its rounded colony has winding ridges and valleys like a brain. Many small polyps share the growing skeleton, building a large dome over many years.
brain-coral.fact: A large brain coral dome can be several centuries old, because it grows only a few millimetres a year.
brain-coral.sourceTitle: University of Florida IFAS — Symmetrical brain coral

golden-coral.text: Chrysogorgia is a genus of branching deep-sea corals with a metallic sheen to their central skeleton. Different species occur in the Pacific and Atlantic, including corals growing on the Titanic. Polyps along their branches capture food from the water. Colony shapes vary among species, from fans and bottlebrushes to bushy forms.
golden-coral.fact: Chrysogorgia golden corals grow branches in spirals, fans or tree-like crowns, depending on the species.
golden-coral.sourceTitle: Pante et al. 2012 — Deep-Sea Origin and In-Situ Diversification of Chrysogorgiid Octocorals

deep-coral.text: A deep-sea sea fan in the genus Paramuricea. These corals form branching, fan-shaped colonies on hard ground in deep water. Their polyps catch food carried by currents. NOAA surveys record Paramuricea on canyon walls and rocky outcrops in the northwest Atlantic, including the Hudson Canyon region.
deep-coral.fact: Paramuricea corals form branching fans on rocky seabeds, where their polyps catch food carried by the current.
deep-coral.sourceTitle: NOAA — Deep coral ecosystems in the northeastern United States

sea-pen.text: A sea pen is a colony of polyps shaped like a quill pen. Its stalk is anchored in soft sediment, and the feeding polyps cluster at the top and catch plankton drifting by.
sea-pen.fact: A sea pen is a colony of polyps anchored in soft sediment by a fleshy stalk. Its feeding polyps catch food from passing water.

facts.Depth: 375 to 1,192 m in the retained OBIS sample

anemone.text: A sea anemone of the deep: a soft muscular column with a crown of stinging tentacles that catch drifting animals. It attaches to rock, wreckage or bones and can slowly change position.
anemone.fact: A deep-sea anemone anchors itself with an adhesive foot and catches prey with stinging tentacles.

sea-lily.text: A stalked crinoid. It anchors to the bottom and holds up a crown of feathery arms to filter food from the current. Crinoids are an ancient group that has lived in the sea for more than 450 million years.
sea-lily.fact: Sea lilies are an ancient group that has lived in the sea for more than 450 million years.

glass-sponge.text: A glass sponge builds its skeleton out of glassy silica needles. It filters bacteria and organic particles from the water, and some deep-sea glass sponges are thought to live for thousands of years.
glass-sponge.fact: Glass sponges build their skeletons from glassy silica needles, and some may live for thousands of years.
glass-sponge.sourceTitle: NOAA — What is a glass sponge?

deepwater-octopus.text: A warty octopus of the North Atlantic. Raised clusters of pale knobs cover its skin, and each arm has a single row of suckers. It lives on the deep continental slope and has no ink sac.
deepwater-octopus.fact: This deep-sea octopus wears a coat of warty bumps across its head and body.

facts.Length: Up to about 50 cm total length (FAO)

deepwater-octopus.sourceTitle: FAO — Cephalopods of the World, Graneledone verrucosa

dumbo-octopus.text: A dumbo octopus swims by flapping a pair of ear-like fins on its mantle and hovers above the seabed, searching for worms and small crustaceans. Species of Grimpoteuthis live from about 400 to well over 6,000 m.
dumbo-octopus.fact: A dumbo octopus swims by flapping ear-like fins and hovers above the seabed.

facts.Depth: Deep sea; a sighting near 7,000 m is confirmed

vampire-squid.text: Neither a squid nor a vampire. It lives in the oxygen-poor midwater, drifts on its fins and sheds glowing mucus from its arm tips instead of ink. It feeds on marine snow it collects with long, sticky filaments.
vampire-squid.fact: The vampire squid is neither squid nor vampire, and it sheds glowing mucus from its arm tips instead of ink.

facts.Depth: Typically 600 to 900 m (MBARI); local OBIS sample 402 to 1,000 m

giant-squid.text: One of the largest invertebrates, with the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, about the size of a dinner plate. It hunts deep fish and squid in the dark, and sperm whales hunt it. It was first filmed alive in the deep sea in 2012.
giant-squid.fact: Scientists first filmed a giant squid in its natural deep-sea habitat in 2012; earlier footage showed one brought to the surface.

sablefish.text: Sablefish, also called black cod, are dark fish of the North Pacific continental slope. Adults live close to muddy bottoms deeper than about 200 metres and feed on fishes and invertebrates.
sablefish.fact: Sablefish, also called black cod, live close to muddy bottoms deeper than about 200 m on the North Pacific slope.

facts.Length: Commonly about 60 to 90 cm; females can exceed 90 cm
facts.Habitat: Continental slope; adults near muddy bottoms
facts.Depth: Adults deeper than about 200 m; species recorded to 2,800 m

sablefish.sourceTitle: NOAA Fisheries — Sablefish; Monterey Bay Aquarium
